title: Antiparticles, neutrinos and beta energy spectra
prior_knowledge_summary: Alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus and gamma radiation have known compositions, masses and charges.
Nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear equations.
Beta-minus and beta-plus emission leave A unchanged and alter Z by one in opposite directions.
new_learning: An antiparticle has the same mass but opposite charge to its corresponding particle, and the positron is the electron antiparticle.
Beta-minus decay emits an electron antineutrino, while beta-plus decay emits an electron neutrino.
Alpha particles have discrete energies, while beta particles have a continuous energy range because energy is shared with an emitted neutrino or antineutrino.
not_yet_taught: hadrons and leptons as particle families

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.heading: Where did the missing beta energy go?
content: Suppose identical nuclei undergo beta-minus decay. If every decay begins and ends with the same nuclear states, we might predict that every emitted electron has the same energy. Experiments show a continuous range instead.
The energy is not lost. Beta decay has another emitted particle, and the available energy is shared.

figure.purpose: Create the missing-energy puzzle from a set of unequal beta energies.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of several identical parent nuclei emitting electrons with visibly different arrow lengths. Put one shared question bubble asking where the remaining energy went. Do not name the unseen particle.
figure.alt_text: Identical beta decays produce electrons with different kinetic energies, creating a missing-energy puzzle.

blocks.heading: Particles can have antiparticles
content: An antiparticle has the same mass but opposite charge to its corresponding particle. The positron is the antiparticle of the electron.

An electron and a positron therefore have equal mass. The electron has charge -e and the positron has charge +e. Opposite charge does not mean opposite mass, and an antiparticle is not simply a particle moving backward.

figure.purpose: Separate the shared and opposite properties in a particle-antiparticle pair.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison card for an electron and positron. Show equal mass on a balance and charges -e and +e in contrasting colours. Include the words same mass and opposite charge only.
figure.alt_text: An electron and positron have the same mass and opposite charges.

blocks.heading: Beta-minus has an antineutrino partner
content: In beta-minus decay, the nucleus emits an electron and an electron antineutrino. Write the extra particle as antineutrino in words when the symbol is not required.
The electron carries charge -e. The antineutrino has zero charge, so adding it does not change the charge bookkeeping learned in the previous lesson. It does carry away energy and momentum.

It may feel as if the electron alone completes the decay because the nuclear A and Z values already balance. That ledger checks nucleon number and charge, but it does not show how energy and momentum are shared.

figure.purpose: Show the complete emitted particle set for beta-minus decay without quark-level detail.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decay sketch with a parent nucleus changing to a daughter, an electron arrow labelled beta-minus and a second arrow labelled electron antineutrino. Add a small charge ledger showing the antineutrino contributes zero charge. No quarks.
figure.alt_text: Beta-minus decay emits an electron and an electron antineutrino.

blocks.heading: Beta-plus has a neutrino partner
content: In beta-plus decay, the nucleus emits a positron and an electron neutrino. The pattern is worth learning as a pair: beta-minus goes with antineutrino, while beta-plus goes with neutrino.

Think of two labelled exit doors. The negative beta door sends out the electron with the anti partner. The positive beta door sends out the positron with the neutrino partner. This memory aid describes the emitted particles without needing the quark model.
Both neutrino and antineutrino are uncharged and have extremely small rest mass. At this level, their key role in the spectrum is that they carry a variable share of energy and momentum.

figure.purpose: Contrast beta-minus and beta-plus emitted pairs.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper split-panel sketch. Left shows beta-minus plus electron antineutrino. Right shows beta-plus plus electron neutrino. Use matching arrows and a simple minus means anti memory cue. Do not include nucleon or quark transformations.
figure.alt_text: Beta-minus is paired with an electron antineutrino and beta-plus with an electron neutrino.

blocks.heading: Why alpha energies appear as lines
content: Consider identical nuclei making the same alpha transition. The main products are the daughter nucleus and alpha particle. For one fixed transition, conservation gives the same available energy each time, divided in one fixed way between these two products.

A detector therefore records a discrete alpha energy for that transition. If a source allows several distinct nuclear transitions, it can produce several separate alpha-energy lines, but each allowed line is still discrete.
The word discrete means separate allowed values rather than every value in between. On an energy plot, draw narrow lines, not a filled continuous band.

figure.purpose: Connect fixed alpha transitions with discrete measured energies.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper sequence from three identical alpha decays to a detector plot with two narrow possible energy lines. Clearly separate event arrows from the spectrum axes. Keep all energy values symbolic.
figure.alt_text: Fixed alpha transitions produce separate narrow energy lines on a spectrum.

blocks.heading: Why beta energies fill a range
content: Imagine a beta-minus decay with 2.40 MeV available as kinetic energy for the emitted electron and antineutrino, ignoring the small recoil only for this teaching example. In one event the electron may receive 0.60 MeV and the antineutrino 1.80 MeV. In another, the electron may receive 1.70 MeV and the antineutrino 0.70 MeV.
Both events conserve energy: 0.60 + 1.80 = 2.40 MeV and 1.70 + 0.70 = 2.40 MeV. Many other divisions are possible, so the electron is measured with a continuous range of energies up to an endpoint.

A common idea is that different beta energies mean energy conservation sometimes fails. The sums show where that idea fails. Each event conserves total energy, but the electron does not receive the whole amount because the antineutrino takes a variable share.

figure.purpose: Make variable energy sharing and event-by-event conservation visible.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout with a 2.40 MeV energy bar split two ways: 0.60 plus 1.80 and 1.70 plus 0.70. Link the electron shares to two positions on a smooth beta spectrum. Include units on every value.
figure.alt_text: Two beta decays share the same available energy differently between an electron and antineutrino.

blocks.heading: Use the emitted-particle set to predict the spectrum
content: First identify the decay. Beta-minus emits an electron and electron antineutrino. Beta-plus emits a positron and electron neutrino. The positron is the electron antiparticle because it has the same mass and opposite charge.

Next ask how many products share the available energy. A fixed alpha transition gives discrete alpha energy. In beta decay, the beta particle and neutrino or antineutrino can divide energy in many ways, giving a continuous beta-energy range.

Finally keep the boundary clear. These conclusions need particle identities, conservation and energy sharing. They do not require quark flavours, hadron classes or quark-level changes, which come later.

figure.purpose: Summarize particle partners and the discrete-versus-continuous decision.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-row summary. Row one pairs beta-minus with antineutrino and beta-plus with neutrino. Row two contrasts fixed alpha energy lines with a continuous beta curve and labels energy sharing as the reason. No answers to practice contexts.
figure.alt_text: A summary links beta partners to continuous spectra and alpha transitions to discrete energies.

concepts_taught: neutrino and antineutrino partners in beta decay
continuous beta energy range from energy sharing
misconceptions_addressed: Balancing A and Z means no other beta-decay particle is needed.
A continuous beta spectrum means energy is not conserved.
next_lesson_can_assume: An antiparticle has the same mass and opposite charge to its particle.
A positron is the electron antiparticle.
Beta-minus emits an electron antineutrino and beta-plus emits an electron neutrino.
Neutrino energy sharing explains the continuous beta-energy range.
Alpha particles from a fixed transition have discrete energies.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Names, charges or compositions of quarks.
Classification of particles as hadrons, baryons, mesons or leptons.
